anti_overlap: fd-emergent-narrative-design-legibility covers player-facing story legibility and gameplay interestingness — this agent covers only bench-instrument validity: reproducibility, discriminative power between policies, and referee-harness integrity.

fd-simulation-calibration-validity-methodology covers general ABM/CSS calibration methodology (identifiability, sample size, reference-class grounding) — this agent covers only the ShadowBench-specific consequences of calibration choices (policy discriminability, byte-identical referee determinism, actor-class attribution needs), not general calibration soundness.
decision_lens: Prioritizes findings where a calibration or trigger-condition choice that looks correct from a game-design or general-calibration lens actually damages ShadowBench's specific requirements: reproducible byte-identical reference streams for the referee harness, sufficient baseline-outcome variance for policies to be discriminable against, and freedom from the anti-gaming concerns already flagged in samsara-trigger-conditions.md (§3 Candidate B's 'tuning_dials(run) = defaults' clause). Deprioritizes pure narrative/legibility findings that don't bear on measurement validity for cross-policy comparison.
focus: Whether the calibration choice (Option A/B/C, and the Samsara trigger-condition candidates A/B/C in the companion doc) preserves or destroys ShadowBench's viability as an alignment-evaluation instrument — specifically reproducibility, discriminative power between decision policies, and freedom from the exact kind of narrow-attractor collapse this calibration effort is trying to fix, given that a bench which discriminates between policies requires the *baseline* (no-intervention) trajectory to be a meaningful reference point that intervention effects can be measured against
name: fd-bench-policy-discriminative-validity
persona: Apply the perspective of an alignment/policy-evaluation benchmark designer — someone who builds evals where the core deliverable is discriminative power between two decision-making policies (e.g., does policy P1 produce measurably different, attributable outcomes than policy P2 on the same task distribution), who treats a benchmark's determinism/reproducibility requirements and its need for outcome variance as being in direct tension (a bench needs the SAME task to be re-runnable for comparison, but needs different POLICIES on that task to produce different, measurable outcomes), and who is trained to distrust any benchmark environment whose baseline dynamics are dominated by a single attractor, because that collapses the effect size available for any policy comparison to noise around a fixed point.
review_areas: Referee re-baseline cost and scope, understated: the jackpot-calibration-brief (§4, Option A) notes 'every trajectory changes ⇒ full referee re-baseline' as a cost, but doesn't address whether the NEW baseline is any more useful as a reference stream than the old bit-identical one — if T₀ becomes seed-dependent, the referee harness (byte-identical determinism check) still works per-seed, but any bench task that reports 'policy P1 changed T₀ by X months relative to baseline' now needs a baseline defined per-seed rather than a single reference point, which is a bench-architecture change the brief doesn't scope, only a re-baseline-the-data-files change

Discriminative power under Option A specifically: if the retuned steady state sits in the Warning band and requires 'compounding seeded shocks' to reach Catastrophe (brief §4), the bench's ability to detect a policy's effect depends on whether policy interventions can plausibly alter which/how-many shocks compound — verify this is mechanically true (does a policy actually have a lever into the demographics→unrest or intrinsic-growth terms, or only into agent-mediated pressures) since if policies can only act through institutional-agent levers (per PHILOSOPHY.md §2: 'deployments affect institutional agents... not pressure values directly') and the retuned collapse is driven by non-agent-mediated deterministic feeds, then no policy can move the needle on T₀ at all, and the bench task 'does policy affect collapse timing' becomes structurally unanswerable regardless of calibration quality

Samsara Candidate B's own named anti-gaming problem generalizes to the calibration ruling itself: samsara-trigger-conditions.md §3 flags that Candidate B's timing window is 'partly a settings artifact... canon-hood would hinge on configuration, not emergence' — the SAME critique applies to Option A's calibration: if the Warning-band target and the decay/growth constants are hand-tuned specifically to produce T₀ in some desired window, the resulting 'seed-dependent T₀' is at risk of being a configuration artifact dressed as emergence, which would fail ShadowBench's reproducibility-with-meaning requirement even while passing the narrower 'not bit-identical' diagnostic — check whether the calibration-sweep plan (§6) includes any check that the retuned system is NOT simply reproducing a narrower version of the same scripted-feeling collapse, i.e. whether it's Golden-Seed-compatible in the bench-validity sense, not just the narrative sense (this is the same failure mode as fd-emergent-narrative-design-legibility's P0 but flagged here specifically as a bench-instrument-validity failure, not a player-experience failure)

Cross-policy comparability of the retuned Chronicle attribution data: the samsara-trigger-conditions doc's Candidate A trigger condition depends on typed attribution (actor_class tags: state/corporate/ngo/player) that doesn't exist yet (§2: 'Attribution is cleared per tick and untyped') — if ShadowBench needs to score 'did this policy change WHO gets attributed for the collapse' as a discriminative signal between policies, and the calibration-effort's chronicle v0 instrumentation doesn't ship actor-class tagging in the same pass, the bench is left able to detect THAT a policy changed the trajectory but not WHY in a policy-attributable way, which weakens discriminative power to a single scalar (T₀ shift) rather than a rich comparison

Interaction between over-damping risk and bench floor effects: if Option A's sweep errs toward the brief's named 'never collapses' failure mode, this doesn't just hurt gameplay (fd-emergent-narrative-design-legibility's concern) — it also produces a bench with a floor effect: if the no-intervention baseline never reaches Catastrophe, any policy that also produces no-Catastrophe outcomes looks identical to the null baseline on the T₀ metric, destroying discriminative power for exactly the policies a safety-relevant bench most wants to distinguish (those that quietly fail to prevent a slow-building crisis vs. those that actively prevent it) — this failure mode needs a bench-specific pass criterion (baseline collapse rate across N seeds must exceed some floor) that is currently absent from the brief's stated sweep-validation plan

Determinism-vs-variance tension left unresolved for the referee harness specifically: the brief says '…the byte-identity harness carries over unchanged — only the reference streams regenerate' (§6) — verify this is actually true once B1 (seeding the emergence RNG) lands: if emergence RNG streams are now seed-dependent where they previously were not, the referee harness's byte-identical check needs the SAME seed to produce the SAME reference stream deterministically for regression testing, which requires the RNG itself to be deterministically seeded (not just 'varied') — confirm the brief's B1 wiring change preserves per-seed determinism (same seed → same trace, forever, across code changes that don't touch emergence) rather than merely introducing variance that could also reintroduce non-reproducibility bugs (e.g., iteration-order-dependent RNG consumption across parallel agent processing, given the 800+ Rayon-parallel agents named in VISION.md)

severity_examples.condition: ShadowBench runs policy-comparison tasks against the retuned baseline and finds zero measurable difference in T₀ or leading-family outcome between any tested policy and the null baseline, not because the policies are equally good but because the collapse mechanism the calibration targeted is structurally unreachable by any agent-mediated intervention — the bench silently loses discriminative power for exactly the systemic-risk scenario (slow-building structural collapse) that matters most for policy evaluation, and this isn't discovered until a policy-comparison study returns a suspicious null result across the board
severity_examples.scenario: Option A retunes deterministic feeds to a Warning-band steady state, but the pressures involved (demographics→unrest, intrinsic economic-strain growth) are not levers any player or scripted policy can act on — per PHILOSOPHY.md, player/policy influence is agent-mediated only, not direct pressure-value modification

severity_examples.condition: The referee harness's byte-identical check starts failing intermittently or after unrelated refactors, and the failure is misdiagnosed as a calibration regression rather than a determinism-infrastructure gap, burning a calibration cycle chasing a non-issue
severity_examples.scenario: B1 (seeding the emergence RNG on the bench path) lands alongside Option A, changing the referee harness's reference streams as noted in the brief, but the RNG consumption order across the 800+ parallel Rayon agent processing pipeline is not guaranteed stable across unrelated future code changes (e.g., agent iteration order, thread scheduling)

severity_examples.condition: The calibration ruling proceeds and locks in a new baseline; a later attempt to build policy-attribution scoring for ShadowBench discovers the tagging gap and has to retrofit actor-class tags onto an already-baselined Chronicle format, creating a second migration that could have been done in the same pass as the calibration's own instrumentation work
severity_examples.scenario: Chronicle v0 instrumentation (per samsara-trigger-conditions §2, shared with the calibration effort) ships pressure/attribution/cascade logging but not the actor-class tagging Candidate A's trigger condition needs

success_hints: The calibration-sweep plan or its successor states an explicit check that at least one policy lever can move T₀ or leading-family outcome in the retuned baseline — i.e., discriminative power is verified, not assumed.
The plan distinguishes 'seed-dependent' (varies with seed) from 'policy-discriminable' (varies with intervention) as two separate validation axes, and validates both.

A floor-effect check (baseline collapse rate across N seeds, post-retune) is included so an over-damped world that never collapses is caught as a bench-validity failure, not just a gameplay flatness complaint.
The B1 RNG-seeding change is verified to preserve same-seed-same-trace determinism under parallel agent execution, not just to introduce seed-to-seed variance.

Actor-class attribution tagging (needed by Samsara Candidate A and by any policy-attribution bench task) is scoped into the same Chronicle-instrumentation pass as the calibration work, rather than deferred to a second migration.
task_context: Design inquiry: gameplay interestingness vs scientific/policy simulation validity for shadow-work's civilizational sim, at its live calibration decision point. Reviewing whether the jackpot-calibration-brief's options and the companion Samsara trigger-condition candidates preserve ShadowBench's viability as a reproducible, policy-discriminative alignment-evaluation instrument. Overall generative goal for this review round: maximize verified novelty×risk surface until dry — answering: what makes for the most interesting gameplay + scientific/policy simulation validity/fidelity for shadow-work?
